title: Magnitude 6.8 at 9:40 a.m.
note: Fictional unit and patients. DRAFT pending clinical sign-off. Your unit protocol, the attending nephrologist and your local disaster authorities decide every real event.
intro: You are the charge nurse of a second-floor unit in Lipa, Batangas. Sixteen patients are connected. The ground starts to shake hard; ceiling panels fall near Station 4.

n1.prompt: What do you and the staff do during the shaking?

choices.text: Stay low beside the nearest patients, shield their heads and steady their access arms, and call out: “Stay connected, cover your head!” Nobody disconnects and nobody runs.
choices.feedback: Protect in place. Disconnecting or moving during shaking causes falls, bleeding and air entry.

choices.text: Start disconnecting the patients nearest the falling panels.
choices.feedback: Disconnecting with unsteady hands during shaking risks bleeding, air in a catheter and lost access.
choices.then: A needle pulls out at Station 4; you press and clamp it as the shaking stops.

choices.text: Run to the exit to open the doors.
choices.feedback: Running during shaking risks falls and leaves patients alone.
choices.then: You fall against a cart; a nurse shields the patients near you.

n2.scene: The shaking stops. A saline pole has tipped at Station 9.
n2.prompt: What do you check, in what order?

choices.text: Every patient first: conscious, breathing, needles and lines secure, no blood at connections. Then machines, then the room (gas, fire, cracks, exits), then count everyone.

vitals.note: Checks done; crack in a column

choices.text: Machines first, to stop the alarms.
choices.feedback: Alarms matter, but a dislodged needle bleeds faster than an alarm harms.

vitals.note: Checks done; crack in a column

choices.text: Go and look at the walls for cracks.
choices.feedback: The building matters, but the patients come first.
choices.then: A nurse calls you back to a bleeding access site at Station 9.

vitals.note: Checks done; crack in a column

n3.scene: The patient at Station 12 is pulling at his lines, shouting to be taken off.

choices.text: Hold his access arm, check his needles, and tell him calmly that staff will take him off if the unit leaves, and that the team is deciding now.
choices.feedback: Calm, specific words prevent the most dangerous self-disconnection.

choices.text: Let him pull his own needles out to calm him.
choices.feedback: Self-disconnection risks bleeding and a lost access, and it panics other patients.
choices.then: His venous needle comes out; you press and clamp the site.

choices.text: Take him off at once, before deciding whether the unit evacuates.
choices.feedback: Ending one session may be reasonable, but act on the stay-or-go decision, with the blood rule.
choices.then: You take him off by protocol once the decision is made.

n4.scene: The facilities officer confirms a new crack across a column on your floor. In the venous line at Station 4, where the panels fell, you see foam.

choices.text: Evacuate: emergency take-off by staff with the blood rule. At Station 4, clamp and do not return the blood (possible air); elsewhere return if quick and safe, or clamp and disconnect; close catheter clamps before separating lines. Then the stairs.
choices.feedback: Visible structural damage means evacuate. Blood that may contain air is never returned.

choices.text: Return everyone’s blood quickly, including Station 4, to save volume.
choices.feedback: Returning a line with foam can push air into the patient.
choices.then: The circuit nurse stops the Station 4 return and clamps the line.

choices.text: Keep the sessions running until the building official arrives.
choices.feedback: With a cracked column and aftershocks expected, staying to finish the schedule risks everyone.
choices.then: An aftershock hits; the incident lead orders the take-off.

end.title: The assembly point
end.text: All sixteen patients and five staff are counted in the parking lot. The building stays closed until a qualified engineer checks it.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • During shaking, protect in place: patients stay connected and covered; staff stay low beside them.
  • After shaking, patients first, then machines, then the building, then a count.
  • The blood rule is the same everywhere: never return blood after air, hemolysis or a severe reaction.
